full_text: Convicted bucks party gang rapists argue guilty verdicts 'unsafe' Sydney men jailed over bucks party gang rape in Newcastle argue guilty verdicts 'unsafe'GBy Giselle WakatamaABC NewcastleTopic:CrimeFri 22 AugFriday 22 AugustFri 22 Aug 2025 at 8:21amComposite Andrew David and Maurice Hawell outside court after their lengthy gang rape trial in 2024. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)In short: Three men jailed over gang rapes in Newcastle are appealing, arguing guilty verdicts were unsafe.Their barristers have argued witnesses were unreliable and have questions directions given to the jury by the presiding judge.What's next?The appellant judges have reserved their decision. abc.net.au/news/convicted-gang-rapists-argue-guilty-verdicts-unsafe-on-appeal/105687344Link copiedShareShare articleLegal teams for a group of men jailed for gang raping three women in Newcastle have argued their guilty verdicts were an unsafe and unsatisfactory verdict , and witnesses were unreliable.Last year brothers Maurice Hawell, 31, and Marius Hawell, 24, and friend Andrew David, 31, were convicted of multiple counts of aggravated sexual assault and aggravated sexual touching in company.The trio's lawyers have spent the past two days challenging the men's convictions and sentences in the Court of Criminal Appeal.An argument around an unsafe verdict alleges the jury's guilty verdict was unsatisfactory and should be overturned.The offences occurred during a bucks weekend in February 2022.The men had travelled to Newcastle and stayed in an Airbnb for the weekend.Two of the women were 18 at the time and the third was 19.'Callous and degrading'In sentencing, Justice Gina O'Rourke said the men engaged in a pack mentality and treated the women in a cold, callous, degrading and criminal way .Maurice Hawell was sentenced to 14 years in prison with a non-parole period of eight years and six months.Maurice Hawell is one of the men appealing his conviction and sentence. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)Andrew David was sentenced to 13 years in prison with a non-parole period of seven years and nine months.Marius Hawell was sentenced to nine years in prison with a non-parole period of five years and five months.The appealThe three men appealed on the grounds the verdicts were unsafe and victims unreliable.The men's barristers also claimed the jury could have been led to misinterpret their state of mind during the bucks weekend.The appellant judges are Justices Stephen Free, Peter Hamill and Belinda Rigg.Crown Prosecutor Bret Hatfield SC today elaborated on the claim about state of mind . The crown says state of mind exists over a 24-hour period and the men were looking for women in nightclubs, Mr Hatfield said.Mr Hatfield added there was a clear a break when the men went and had breakfast and went sightseeing in Newcastle.The court heard it was Andrew David's bucks party. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)The men's barristers also took aim at the credibility of witnesses on the Friday night and their understanding of consent.Mr Hatfield today told the judges there should not be expectations about how complainants in sexual assault matters should behave .'Inconsistencies'He said inconsistencies in their evidence largely relates to the number of people walking back to the apartment [where they were staying] and how many men were outside the room when they were being sexually assaulted. They have visceral and graphic detail that is hard to make up and embellish, Mr Hatfield said.He said that inconsistencies were relevant of course, but they were not significant .The presiding trial judge ruled against separate trials due to the context of the evidence.The men met two of the women at Newcastle's Cambridge Hotel. full_text: Magistrate convicts police officer who punched teen during arrest Magistrate finds police officer assaulted teen during arrest in Batemans BayBy Christien de GarisABC South East NSWTopic:CourtsFri 22 AugFriday 22 AugustFri 22 Aug 2025 at 8:11amBrett David Lindsay outside Batemans Bay Local Court. (ABC South East NSW: Christien De Garis)In short:A Senior Constable has been found guilty of using unreasonable force during the arrest of two teenage boys in Batemans Bay.Brett David Lindsay punched a 17-year-old boy during the arrest, with the magistrate finding the officer had no intention of de-escalating the situation .What's next?He was sentenced to two-year community correction order.abc.net.au/news/police-officer-assaulted-teen-batemans-bay-arrest-court-finds/105684886Link copiedShareShare articleA New South Wales police officer has been found guilty of assault and using an unreasonable amount of force during the arrest of two teenage boys in Batemans Bay.The case centred on the way Senior Constable Brett David Lindsay forced the then 14 and 17-year-old boys to the ground during the arrest in October 2023.Lindsay described using a distraction strike when he punched the older boy's collarbone.In Batemans Bay Local Court on Friday, Magistrate Doug Dick said he was satisfied the use of force was unnecessary. It was a use of force no reasonable officer would have used in the circumstances, he said.Investigating home invasionThe court heard Senior Constable Lindsay and his partner were investigating claims of a potential home invasion in Batemans Bay, which led them to a block of units where several teenagers were.Senior Constable Lindsay told the court they suspected the teenagers were involved in the alleged home invasion and arrested them.Over the two-day hearing, prosecutors pointed to body-worn camera footage which captured Senior Constable Lindsay grabbing the younger boy by his shoulders and throwing him onto a concrete floor.Brett David Lindsay's hearing took place in the Batemans Bay Local Court. (ABC News: James Tugwell)It also showed when a scuffle broke out between Senior Constable Lindsay and the 17-year-old, where the officer ended up on top of the teenager.Senior Constable Lindsay told the court the teenager tensed up, and he feared the boy was in reach of his gun and handcuffs, so he struck him on his collarbone area. I used what I would call a distraction strike … hopefully change [the teenager's] demeanour and direction it was heading, he said.The older teenager then repeatedly called the officer a white gronk and a f***ing dog .Giving evidence, the 17-year-old said: I didn't think a copper would hit me at that age. The court was told in another interaction, the police officer forced the 17-year-old to the ground, with his knee coming into contact with the teenager's stomach.Senior Constable Lindsay testified the teenager then clenched his fist.The Batemans Bay Senior Constable pleaded not guilty to six charges. (ABC News: James Tugwell)On the body-worn camera footage, the police officer can be heard saying to the teen: Do you want a f***ing punch mate, you'll get one. Magistrate rejects evidenceIn delivering his verdict, Magistrate Dick said it was clear [the 17-year-old] held ill feeling towards all police … [he] was deliberately confrontational and hostile .However, he went on to say he did not believe Senior Constable Lindsay's evidence that the officer genuinely believed he used necessary force. [Senior Constable Lindsay] had no intention of de-escalating the situation … [he] downplayed the seriousness of his conduct, Magistrate Dick said.Brett David Lindsay was given a community correction order. (ABC South East NSW: Christien De Garis)In sentencing, Senior Constable Lindsay's defence lawyer Ahmad Moutasallem revealed his client was suffering post-traumatic stress disorder and was on medical leave, as well as being suspended from the police force. He will not be working as a police officer anymore, Mr Moutasallem said.Magistrate Dick recorded a criminal conviction against the three assault charges and ordered Senior Constable Lindsay to serve a two-year community correction order.A NSW Police spokesperson confirmed Senior Constable Lindsay remained suspended with pay and a review would now be conducted.ABC South East NSW — local news in your inboxGet our local newsletter, delivered free each ThursdayEmail addressSubscribeYour information is being handled in accordance with the ABC Privacy Collection Statement.Posted Fri 22 Aug 2025 at 8:11amFriday 22 Aug 2025 at 8:11amFri 22 Aug 2025 at 8:11amShare optionsCopy linkFacebookX (formerly Twitter)Top StoriesAustralia Post halts most parcel postage to US immediatelyTopic:Postal and Delivery ServicesPhoto shows White postal sack with red express post labellingPM, Wong expected to make significant foreign affairs announcementLIVEPhoto shows Penny Wong looks at Anthony Albanese at a press conferneceMillions of Australians will not have a say in who inherits their superannuation Topic:SuperannuationPhoto shows A lady's hands shown close up holding a letter from Aus SuperHe's at the centre of a major fraud investigation. full_text: Men charged over alleged plot to import 185 kg of methamphetamine into WA Perth men charged over alleged plot to import 185 kg of methamphetamine, attempt to steal $300kBy Nicolas PerpitchTopic:CrimeFri 22 AugFriday 22 AugustFri 22 Aug 2025 at 8:05amAuthorities discovered 185 kilograms of meth hidden in bags of rice. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)In short:Police have charged a Perth man with trying to import 185 kilograms of methamphetamine into WA.The drugs were seized in bags of rice sent by sea from Pakistan.He and another Perth man have been charged over an alleged conspiracy to steal $300,000 in cash from two Victorians accused of trying to smuggle the money out of WA.abc.net.au/news/wa-perth-drug-cash-haul-/105686958Link copiedShareShare articleIt's a rare insight into Perth's violent organised criminal underworld.Authorities have lifted the lid on an operation that stopped 185 kilograms of methamphetamine hitting the streets and foiled a suspected plot by the alleged drug traffickers to also steal $300,000 in illicit cash off a Victorian man and woman in an armed highway heist.Police allege the Victorians were trying to smuggle the crime money out of Western Australia.In dramatic footage, officers can be seen pulling over a white van with suspects inside in the outer Perth suburb of Wooroloo on August 5. Show me your hands, put your hands out of the window now! One officer yells to the occupants as he approaches the car. Passenger, open the window! Hands out! Do not move! Do not move for anything, do you understand me? Loading...Police handcuff a man and pull him out of the van and onto the grass next to the road.An officer removes a loaded handgun from the front of the man's tracksuit pants.He takes the magazine out of the gun and puts it in an evidence bag.The video then shows officers searching the boot of a car and pulling out two vacuum sealed clear plastic bags from a hidden compartment, full of crisp $50 notes.Police allege the men involved had clear links to organised crime networks with international connections and outlaw motorcycle gangs.Operation Estevan was conducted by the WA Joint Organised Crime taskforce, involving the Australian Federal Police, WA Police, Australian Border Force, Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission and AUSTRAC.Information from the investigation yesterday led police to a home in the northern Perth suburb of Nollamara, where they arrested a man after finding a point-22 handgun, a sawn-off shotgun, hundreds of rounds of ammunition, knuckledusters, banned knives, methamphetamine, cannabis and other drugs.Significant discoveryThe operation started in December 2024, when authorities discovered 185 kilograms of meth hidden in bags of rice in a consignment sent by sea from Pakistan.That's the equivalent of 1.8 million street deals and would have been worth about $171 million to the criminal group.But AFP Assistant Commissioner Pryce Scanlan said the drug seizure has hurt the syndicate and left them potentially vulnerable. They obviously owe a lot of money potentially offshore. But this puts a big dent into organised crime, he said.A package containing methamphetamine which authorities will allege was found in a bag of rice. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)A 35-year-old man from the Perth suburb of Doubleview has subsequently been charged with importing a commercial quantity of methamphetamine, a charge that carries a maximum penalty of life imprisonment.He's due in the Perth Magistrates court next week.Police then received intelligence tipping them off to what they call a threat to life .'Highway robbery'Police allege the Doubleview man and a 35-year-old man from the Perth suburb of Gwelup hatched a plan to execute what we can only refer to as a highway robbery .WA Police assistant commissioner Tony Longhorn said their target was the Victorian man and woman allegedly trying to smuggle $300,000 in cash gained through crime out of the state in a car.The two Perth men had allegedly placed tracking devices on the Victorians' vehicle and knew exactly where they would be. It is alleged that the drug traffickers planned to stop the couriers on the highway at gunpoint and steal the cash, assistant commissioner Longhorn said. It wasn't going to take place in a dark back street. This was going to be open air. Midday. With the community at risk. And we all know how this could have gone if it had gone wrong. Police say the meth haul had a value of about $171 million. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)Police allege one of the men had a loaded handgun when he was arrested.The two Perth men have been charged with one count each of conspiracy to commit an indictable offence, unlawful possession of a firearm, and one count of possessing money from the proceeds of crime.The two Victorians were charged with the same offence.WA 'hostile' to organised crimeAFP assistant commissioner Scanlan said it showed the links between illicit drugs and violent crime. These people are the ones who are preying on our children, your friends, your neighbours, trying to get them hooked onto these insidious drugs and turn them into people you do not recognise, he said. People who will rob, lie, steal and cheat. We're making WA as hostile as possible, and make sure drugs aren't coming through our borders. The 41-year-old man was arrested in bushland in Perth. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)In other recent operations, earlier this month a 41-year-old Coffin Cheaters Outlaw motorcycle gang member and a 34-year-old associate were charged after they were caught allegedly collecting 30 kilograms of methamphetamine in tea packaging from Perth bushland.Police say they were arrested after a lengthy foot chase, and they seized a hessian bag from one man allegedly containing a shovel, night vision goggles and a dedicated encrypted communications device.The 34 year old man was arrested after a lengthy police pursuit. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)Police also seized 15 kilograms of methamphetamine hidden in wooden furniture that arrived in Fremantle from South Africa earlier this year, with a street value close to $14 million.A Sydney man, who had flown to Perth the day before, has been charged with one count of importing a commercial quantity of border-controlled drugs.LoadingPosted Fri 22 Aug 2025 at 8:05amFriday 22 Aug 2025 at 8:05amFri 22 Aug 2025 at 8:05amShare optionsCopy linkFacebookX (formerly Twitter)Top StoriesAustralia Post halts most parcel postage to US immediatelyTopic:Postal and Delivery ServicesPhoto shows White postal sack with red express post labellingPM, Wong expected to make significant foreign affairs announcementLIVEPhoto shows Penny Wong looks at Anthony Albanese at a press conferneceMillions of Australians will not have a say in who inherits their superannuation Topic:SuperannuationPhoto shows A lady's hands shown close up holding a letter from Aus SuperHe's at the centre of a major fraud investigation. full_text: 'Sorry and sordid tale': WA GP jailed for child sex offences WA GP Douglas William McCarthy jailed for child sex offencesDBy David WeberTopic:CourtsFri 22 AugFriday 22 AugustFri 22 Aug 2025 at 7:03amDouglas McCarthy was sentenced for a range of sexual offences against teenage girls. (ABC News: Dave Weber)In short: Douglas William McCarthy, 63, who was a practising GP when he paid underage girls for sex has been sentenced to 20 years in jail. Judge Wendy Gillan rejected his evidence that he did not know the ages of most of the girls and said he should have known better given his age, intelligence and education.What's next? He'll be eligible for parole after 18 years.abc.net.au/news/wa-gp-douglas-william-mccarthy-sentenced-for-child-sex-/105686986Link copiedShareShare articleA West Australian doctor who paid tens of thousands of dollars to teenage girls for sex and photos, and kept a video library of his offending, has been sentenced to 20 years in prison.WARNING: This article contains details some readers may find distressing.Douglas William McCarthy, 63, was a practising GP in the state's south west, when he engaged in sexual acts with girls aged 14 and 15.McCarthy was found guilty by a WA District Court jury last week of a range of offences, including persistent sexual conduct and sexual penetration, possessing child pornography, and encouraging a 17-year-old to engage in prostitution.He was also found guilty of attempting to pervert the course of justice after paying some of his victims to keep quiet , including depositing $800 into one of the girls' bank accounts.If you or anyone you know needs help:1800 RESPECT national helpline on 1800 737 732Sexual Assault Counselling Australia on 1800 211 028Bravehearts (support for child sexual abuse survivors) on 1800 272 831Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380Lifeline (24 hour crisis line) on 131 114'Sordid and sorry tale'In a scathing sentencing hearing, District Judge Wendy Gillan said McCarthy was only interested in his own selfish desires and described his offending over more than two years as a sorry and sordid tale .Judge Gillan said McCarthy, whose sexual involvement with the girls started when he was aged in his late fifties, engaged in a high level of corruption and should have known better given his age, intelligence and education.Douglas McCarthy has been jailed for 20 years. (ABC News: David Weber)She rejected his evidence that he didn't know the ages of most of the girls. Their true age was not an impediment to you, she said, pointing out that they were intoxicated during the sexual acts.One girl was 14 when she first posed for photos and sent them to McCarthy after being told by a friend that he would pay for them.This led to her going to see him and being paid for sexual acts, in what was a familiar pattern for other victims.In other incidents, he recorded videos of the offending, many of which the judge said were degrading .Judge Gillan said he'd allowed teenage girls to drink alcohol, take MDMA and smoke marijuana in his presence, including at his home. Your house was a party house where young people were able to use drugs with impunity. Victim impact statementsThe court heard that five of the teenagers had provided victim impact statements, with one saying McCarthy had stolen her innocence and she had been made to feel like a cheap prostitute .Another said she now found it difficult to trust older men and to speak with doctors.McCarthy's lawyer Wayne Burg referred to a letter his client had provided for the judge, saying he now believed the girls are blameless and he takes responsibility for his actions .But prosecutor Sean Stocks said last week those girls weren't blameless , telling the court that there was no remorse, just manipulation .Prosecutor Sean Stocks said McCarthy was not remorseful. full_text: Podcaster faces murder charge over death of 30yo Perth woman Tobias Marcus Nuttall faces Perth court charged with murder of woman in BassendeanKBy Kenith PngTopic:CourtsFri 22 AugFriday 22 AugustFri 22 Aug 2025 at 7:00amTobias Nuttall has been charged with murder over the death of a 30-year-old woman in Bassendean. (YouTube)In short:A Perth conspiracy podcaster, Tobias Marcus Nuttall, has been charged with murder over the death of a 30-year-old woman in Bassendean.He appeared briefly in Midland Magistrates Court, speaking only to confirm his name, and will remain in custody until a September court date.Police say the woman was found critically injured at a Reid Street home on Wednesday, later dying in hospital as homicide detectives continue investigating.abc.net.au/news/tobias-marcus-nuttall-faces-court-charged-with-bassendean-murder/105684606Link copiedShareShare articleA conspiracy theorist podcaster has appeared in court charged with murder over the death of a 30-year-old woman in Perth's eastern suburbs.Tobias Marcus Nuttall, 32, appeared in the Midland Magistrates court today in custody, wearing a blue jumpsuit, with a beard and long hair.Mr Nuttall is accused of killing the woman, who is believed to be known to him, in Bassendean on Wednesday.The scene was cordoned off by police as they investigated the woman's death. (ABC News: Lily Kristanto)In court, Mr Nuttall did not speak, other than to confirm his name.No further information was given by prosecutors, and Mr Nuttall will remain in custody ahead of his next court appearance in September.The WA Police Homicide Squad are investigating the woman's death, after emergency crews rushed to a house on Reid Street just after midday, finding a woman who had sustained critical injuries.Police were called to the house on Reid Street on Wednesday afternoon. (ABC News: Lily Kristanto)She was rushed to Royal Perth Hospital where she died.Deep dive podcastMr Nuttall co-hosts an online podcast which is branded as a deep dive into the realms of conspiracy, the occult, magic, spirituality, and everything clandestine. As two inquisitive minds on a quest for truth, they pull back the curtains of the mundane to reveal a world bubbling with mysteries, hidden agendas, and esoteric knowledge, the podcast description says.Tobias Nuttall appearing on a podcast. (YouTube)On an episode posted on Wednesday night, after the alleged murder took place, Mr Nuttall's co-host excused his absence. There's nothing wrong with Toby, his co-host said.The 32-year-old was a co-host of a podcast that had last posted an episode on the day of the alleged murder. (YouTube) Toby had an appointment he had to come over to Sydney for and he was flying back from Sydney to Perth today. This is just to tell everybody we won't be doing one with Toby tonight, we'll have to do that tomorrow. Mr Nuttall was charged with murder the following evening.The charges were referenced by the co-host in a later episode.“Toby has been charged …. with a very very serious offence over in Perth, something that happened on Wednesday, the co-host said.Supporters of Tobias Marcus Nuttall outside the Midland Magistrates Court on Friday. full_text: Illicit tobacco, money laundering funding Victorian burglaries, arsons Seizure of $7.2 million worth of illicit tobacco is linked to an alleged Iraqi crime syndicateTopic:CrimeFri 22 AugFriday 22 AugustFri 22 Aug 2025 at 6:00amPolice intercepted a truck in Laverton North allegedly carrying $5 million of illicit tobacco. (Supplied: Victoria Police)abc.net.au/news/two-men-arrested-seven-million-dollars-illicit-tobacco/105686114Link copiedShareShare articleVictorian police say the seizure of $7.2 million worth of illicit tobacco is linked to an alleged Iraqi crime syndicate that is laundering money and using it to fund serious offending like aggravated burglaries.Police said they became aware an organised crime syndicate was conducting cash drops and collections at a small takeaway shop in Somerton, in Melbourne's north, in January. They also said further transactions were taking place at a factory in Epping. On Thursday Victoria Police, along with the Australian Border Force, executed warrants at two homes in Dallas and a business in Epping, where they seized $1.9 million worth of illicit tobacco, $80,000 in cash and six high-end watches. A 40-year-old Dallas man was arrested and is expected to be charged with possession of a commercial quantity of illicit tobacco and knowingly dealing with the proceeds of crime.Police believe over $83 million of cash has been laundered since May 2021.Victoria Police said as part of a separate investigation they intercepted a truck carrying $5 million of illegal cigarettes in Laverton North.The alleged driver, a 34-year-old Cambellfield man, was arrested at his home on Thursday, where detectives seized $100,000 in cash.Police said they believed the man attended the same Somerton shop linked to the money laundering investigation, and has alleged links to the organised crime syndicate involved. 'Vast number of crimes' can be committed with millions of dollarsDetective Inspector Graham Banks from Victoria Police said the seizures were significant. This group is connected to Iraqi organised crime entities, and they're funnelling money offshore to people who are directing very serious crimes in Victoria and the rest of Australia, he said.Detective Inspector Banks said to put the money into context, $1 million could buy a criminal syndicate 400 stolen cars. A million dollars will pay for 100 arsonists, a million dollars will buy you about 40 semi-automatic pistols with rounds, or if you prefer 20 assault rifles, he said. A million dollars will probably pay for two underworld hits of mid-level underworld characters, sometimes it goes up to $1 million. So there's $4 million, and there's a vast number of crimes that can committed with that money. But it doesn't speak to the money behind the crime, or the houses that have been broken into and the hundreds of people who have been victims of aggravated home invasions, or the large number of businesses that have had their businesses destroyed who aren't even related to the illicit tobacco trade. Syndicates using apps to hire criminalsDetective Inspector Banks said the crimes were organised on encrypted apps like Signal and WhatsApp. And people take up contracts, sometimes very small in monetary value, to do very serious offending, he said.Detective Inspector Graham Banks says criminals are being hired using encrypted apps. (ABC News)He said the amount of money that had been generated by the illicit tobacco trade was really staggering , and it was equal to, or more than, the drug trade.Detective Inspector Banks said there were one or two syndicates driving it. They will be the focus [of police]. They are the people who are killing people, they are the people organising arsons and they people who are organising aggravated burglaries which are impacting all members of the community, he said.Posted Fri 22 Aug 2025 at 6:00amFriday 22 Aug 2025 at 6:00amFri 22 Aug 2025 at 6:00amShare optionsCopy linkFacebookX (formerly Twitter)Top StoriesAustralia Post halts most parcel postage to US immediatelyTopic:Postal and Delivery ServicesPhoto shows White postal sack with red express post labellingPM, Wong expected to make significant foreign affairs announcementLIVEPhoto shows Penny Wong looks at Anthony Albanese at a press conferneceMillions of Australians will not have a say in who inherits their superannuation Topic:SuperannuationPhoto shows A lady's hands shown close up holding a letter from Aus SuperHe's at the centre of a major fraud investigation. full_text: 'Blind drunk' driver jailed for 14 years over hit and run death of 43yo mum Drunk driver Brett Eddy imprisoned for 14 years over manslaughter of Fraser Coast woman Natasha RavenBy Talissa SigantoTopic:CrimeFri 22 AugFriday 22 AugustFri 22 Aug 2025 at 5:51amNatasha Raven died after being struck by the vehicle Brett Eddy was driving. (Supplied)In short:Drunk driver Brett Eddy has been sentenced to 14 years' jail for the hit and run death of 43-year-old Natasha Raven last year.Ms Raven's family and friends told the Supreme Court in Brisbane of the pain they have been living with since her death.What's next?Eddy will be eligible for parole in 2033.abc.net.au/news/brett-eddy-imprisoned-for-manslaughter-drink-driver/105686842Link copiedShareShare articleA driver who was blind drunk and travelling at extreme speed when he killed a pedestrian in a hit and run on Queensland's Fraser Coast has been sentenced to 14 years in jail.Brett Eddy, 42, pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court in Brisbane on Friday to several charges, including the manslaughter of Natasha Raven.The 43-year-old was struck by a car being driven by Eddy and left for dead on a Urangan street late at night in May last year. Eddy pleaded guilty in the Supreme Court in Brisbane on Friday. (Supplied)During a sentencing hearing, the court heard the day in question had been Eddy's birthday, and he had been drinking heavily throughout the day.The court heard at around 10pm, after being removed from a licensed venue, he drove to a friend's home who described him as being loud and obnoxious and blind drunk .He continued drinking, and around two hours later, the court heard he drove to a convenience store with a child, where staff said he was f*****g hammered .Court hears child filmed 'drunken joyride'Crown prosecutor Stephen Muir told the court Eddy then went on a drunken joyride , reaching speeds of up to 180 kilometres an hour through suburban streets. He should have been nowhere near behind the wheel of a car, he said.Mr Muir told the court Eddy reprehensibly then had the child film his dangerous driving, which was played to the court. That recording captures the defendant's obvious enjoyment in the moments before the killing, he said.The court heard at similar extreme speed he entered the shoulder of the road where Ms Raven was walking, just metres from her home, before he hit her and fled the scene.Ms Raven died at the scene of the crash. (ABC News)'Your actions are unforgivable'Ms Raven's brother Josh Raven submitted a victim impact statement to the court which was read by the prosecution.In his statement he said Eddy was a nightmare that lives in my head . The pain you've caused me is beyond anything I've already experienced, he said. Your actions are unforgivable. Mr Raven told the court the images, thoughts and smells from the crash scene will haunt me for the rest of my life . I hope this lives in your head for as long as you may live, he said to Eddy.Ms Raven's best friend Lauren Richards read her victim impact statement to the court.She said her death had left me with a pain I will carry for the rest of my life . Since she's been gone, I have been so alone, she said.Ms Richards told the court the death had taken the hardest toll on Ms Raven's son who is broken by grief and headed down the wrong path. Every day I watch him struggle and it tears me apart, she said. He feels lost without his Mum and he doesn't see much for his life ahead. Eddy appeared in court via video link on Friday. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)Driver tells court 'I will never forgive myself'Appearing in court via video link from prison Eddy apologised to the Raven family and through tears said: I'll never forgive myself . I'm so sorry for this, I shouldn't have been on the road and it's my fault that this has happened, he said. I don't wish for anyone to forgive me, but I just want everyone to know that I am so sorry. The court heard Eddy had a lengthy criminal record across three states which spanned decades, and that he had a highly relevant traffic history of repeated unlicensed and drink driving offending.Justice Peter Davis took into consideration Eddy had entered into timely pleas and accepted other mitigating factors such as a PTSD diagnosis.However, when determining his sentence, he said Eddy exhibited “a high level of criminality” which caused Ms Raven, who was “innocent in all this” to lose her life in “violent circumstances”.“The nature of your driving was outrageously reckless,” he said.Eddy will be eligible for parole in 2033.Posted Fri 22 Aug 2025 at 5:51amFriday 22 Aug 2025 at 5:51amFri 22 Aug 2025 at 5:51am, updated Fri 22 Aug 2025 at 6:02amFriday 22 Aug 2025 at 6:02amFri 22 Aug 2025 at 6:02amShare optionsCopy linkFacebookX (formerly Twitter)Top StoriesAustralia Post halts most parcel postage to US immediatelyTopic:Postal and Delivery ServicesPhoto shows White postal sack with red express post labellingPM, Wong expected to make significant foreign affairs announcementLIVEPhoto shows Penny Wong looks at Anthony Albanese at a press conferneceMillions of Australians will not have a say in who inherits their superannuation Topic:SuperannuationPhoto shows A lady's hands shown close up holding a letter from Aus SuperHe's at the centre of a major fraud investigation. (Supplied: NSW Police)In short: A 56-year-old postal worker is accused of stealing bank cards and other items from mail in Sydney's east.Police allege he supplied the stolen cards to two separate criminal syndicates, resulting in $1.4 million worth of fraud.Two other men were charged in connection and all three men are due before court next month.abc.net.au/news/nsw-sydney-postal-worker-charged-over-alleged-bank-fraud/105685680Link copiedShareShare articleA Sydney postman has been charged with the alleged mail theft of bank cards and other items in Sydney's east, resulting in $1.4 million worth of fraud.Police from the Financial Crimes Squad allege the 56-year-old postman supplied the stolen bank cards to two separate criminal syndicates.The postman allegedly stole items from 70 letters or packages in Edgecliff, Woollahra and Double Bay in the city's east, with police and Australia Post last November launching a joint investigation.Strike Force Detectives on Wednesday with help from NSW Police's organised crime squad Raptor executed five search warrants in Rockdale in Sydney's south and Roselands in the city's south west. During the warrants, police allegedly located and seized more than $14,000 in cash, a Dedicated Encrypted Criminal Communication Device, electronics, stolen bank cards, a taser, and luxury items including watches, handbags and jewellery, NSW Police said in a statement.56-year-old postman Mauro Coluzzi was then arrested in his home in Rockdale, along with two other men at separate locations.He was charged by police with 143 counts of dishonestly obtaining financial advantage by deception, stealing items from 70 pieces of mail, and participating in a criminal group.Police seized more than $14,000 in cash after executing five search warrants. (Supplied: NSW Police)The postman appeared before Sutherland Local Court on Thursday where he was granted conditional bail, including surrendering his passport.The other two men charged in connection with the alleged theft and fraud — 35-year-old Ashish Tamrakar from Rockdale and 27-year-old Ibrahim Abbas from Roselands — have also been granted bail.All three men are due before court next month.Alleged thefts reported by concerned banksNSW Financial Crimes Squad Commander, Detective Acting Superintendent Con Galea, said two of the three men were known to police previously. They were known to each other; they had an association from the time we were investigating them. Two of them — including the postman — were known to police. He said the alleged thefts were initially reported by the banks. The reporting happened in mid last year [2024] and several hundred customers have been affected. Acting Superintendent Galea said the criminal syndicates were allegedly involved in fraud. Basically, the criminal syndicates are focusing on fraud and deception related offences, obtaining those cards and perpetrating other frauds using those cards. Australia Post confirmed it has been supporting NSW Police in their investigation. (ABC South East NSW: Fatima Olumee)Police said the amount of money allegedly defrauded is expected to increase, as police investigate further cases from the alleged theft of the bank cards.In a statement, a spokesperson for Australia Post said more than 2.3 billion items are delivered through its network each year. Australia Post is proud of the role it plays in delivering for the community. This is a very serious matter and Australia Post has been supporting NSW Police in their investigation — and will continue to do so. Given the matter is before the Courts, it is not appropriate for us to comment further, Australia Post said.The ABC understands the postman has been suspended from his duties pending the investigation.Posted Fri 22 Aug 2025 at 4:56amFriday 22 Aug 2025 at 4:56amFri 22 Aug 2025 at 4:56amShare optionsCopy linkFacebookX (formerly Twitter)Top StoriesAustralia Post halts most parcel postage to US immediatelyTopic:Postal and Delivery ServicesPhoto shows White postal sack with red express post labellingPM, Wong expected to make significant foreign affairs announcementLIVEPhoto shows Penny Wong looks at Anthony Albanese at a press conferneceMillions of Australians will not have a say in who inherits their superannuation Topic:SuperannuationPhoto shows A lady's hands shown close up holding a letter from Aus SuperHe's at the centre of a major fraud investigation. full_text: Miami-Dade deputy charged in UPS driver’s death claims Stand Your Ground Crime Miami-Dade deputy charged in UPS driver’s death claims Stand Your Ground By Charles Rabin Updated August 23, 2025 11:02 AM Defendant Jose Mateo with his lawyer Carlos Salazar argues Florida’s Stand-Your-Ground statute before Judge Ernest A. Kollra on Friday, Aug. 22, 2025. Mateo is one of four Miami-Dade police officers charged with manslaughter in the case stemming from the death of UPS driver Frank Ordonez, who was shot by police during a shootout with his kidnappers in Broward in 2019. (Mike Stocker/South Florida Sun Sentinel) Mike Stocker South Florida Sun Sentinel A police officer charged in the gunfire deaths of two innocent bystanders during a shootout at a busy intersection six years ago is taking a novel approach in a last-ditch effort to avoid trial: He wants the charges dropped based on Florida’s Stand Your Ground statute — even though he’s not charged with killing the suspected gunmen.Suspended Miami-Dade Sheriff’s deputy Jose Mateo, 33, who pleaded not guilty to manslaughter along with three other officers last year in the shooting death of a UPS truck driver and a man stuck in traffic, argued in Broward County Circuit Court Friday that he is protected by the state’s Stand Your Ground and fleeing felon laws and that the charges against him should be dismissed. His trial is scheduled to begin next week.The Stand Your Ground statute allows a person — and police officers — in Florida to take up to deadly action if they feel their life is threatened. The fleeing felon law allows police to shoot at a suspect if they believe that person is a danger to society while trying to avoid custody.The roughly 90-minute argument before Broward Circuit Court Judge Ernest Krolla Jr. came down to whether an officer should receive immunity under those statutes for the accidental killing of an innocent bystander. State prosecutor Chuck Morton, using an example of a civilian shooting at a would-be robber and accidentally killing someone taking a walk, said it should not. Morton said the self-defense argument only holds water if Mateo were charged in the shooting death of the two men accused of committing the crimes.“You need to be prudent when shooting into crowds,” said Morton, a Broward County assistant state attorney.Mateo’s attorney Richard Diaz argued the killing of an innocent bystander while police are shooting at someone firing in a crowd should get the same consideration of “transfer of intent” as a criminal being charged for the shooting death of someone by accident. He also told the judge, either way, his decision Monday would be “groundbreaking law.”“The Legislature never wrote into the statute whether it does apply, or doesn’t apply,” Diaz said. Richard Diaz, attorney for Jose Mateo, argues Florida’s Stand-Your-Ground statute before Judge Ernest A. Kollra on Friday, Aug. 22, 2025. Mateo is one of four Miami-Dade officers charged with manslaughter in the case stemming from the death of UPS driver Frank Ordonez, who was shot by police during a shootout with his kidnappers in Broward in December 2019. Mike Stocker South Florida Sun Sentinel Krolla didn’t appear to be leaning in any direction, but did question Morton repeatedly on whether an officer should shoot into a crowded situation — like a football game — to subdue an active shooter. He said he’d have a decision by Monday.A Florida Department of Law Enforcement investigation completed last year found that the six bullets that killed carjacked UPS truck driver Frank Ordonez, 27, and and Rick Cutshaw, 70, the bystander and former union organizer who was stuck in traffic that day, came from the guns of four Miami-Dade police officers.Mateo and three other Miami-Dade Sheriff’s deputies, Richard Santiesteban, 40, Leslie Lee, 58 and Rodolfo Mirabal, 39, were indicted of manslaughter in Broward County in June 2024. All pleaded not guilty and all have been suspended without pay.More than 90 bullets fired during shootoutOrdóñez and Cutshaw lost their lives in a hail of gunfire in the packed intersection of Miramar Parkway and Flamingo Road during the 5 p.m. rush hour in December 2019.Nearly 90 bullets were fired during the raging gun battle that involved more than a dozen officers from four agencies — and which was filmed live by television choppers flying overhead.An investigation by the FDLE last August determined five bullets from Miami-Dade police officers were uncovered during Ordóñez’s autopsy. Two linked to back to Santiesteban, and the rest to Mateo, Lee and Mirabal. A single bullet was recovered during Cutshaw’s autopsy. That one was tied to Mirabal, the report states.Also killed that day were Lamar Alexander and Ronnie Jerome Hill, two ex-cons whose exploits that day began with a bungled attempt to rob a Coral Gables jewelry store.The investigation found Santiesteban fired at least 44 times; Mirabal 19; Mateo 18 and Lee, six. In all, 20 Miami-Dade officers, three Miramar officers, one Pembroke Pines officer and one Florida Highway Patrol trooper were involved in the shootout that began earlier that day when a robbery at a Coral Gables jewelry store went awry.Botched jewelry heist led to tragedyThe unlikely course of events that led to the four deaths on Dec. 19, 2024, began in the late afternoon at Regent Jewelers on Miracle Mile in Coral Gables. When the robbery soured, Hill and Alexander raced from the store and hijacked the UPS truck driven by Ordóñez - with the driver still in it. Yellow tape blocks the access to the sidewalk after a robbery at Regent Jewelers at 386 Miracle Mile in Coral Gables on Dec. 5, 2019. The shootout in Broward County - that left a UPS driver and bystander dead - began with a bungled robbery attempt at Regent Jewelers. The robbers carjacked the UPS truck in the Gables - with the driver in it - and fled into Broward, where multiple police agencies engaged in a shootout amid rush-hour traffic. Pedro Portal pportal@miamiherald.com That ignited a high-speed chase up the Florida Turnpike, on Okeechobee Road and Interstate 75 — with gunfire being exchanged — and to the busy rush-hour streets of Pembroke Pines. There, the UPS truck and police cars from several agencies got stuck in a traffic jam and officers and the kidnappers began a blistering gun battle caught live on television station cameras hovering overhead.Bullets from police weapons struck several unintended targets, the FDLE report found. Some fired by Mirabal struck two vehicles, hitting a dashboard and a car seat. Four from Mateo’s weapon hit the rear bumper of another vehicle. Body camera footage also showed Mirabal stopping his cruiser behind the passenger side of the UPS truck and firing his weapon.The report said Mateo got out of his patrol vehicle and walked toward the passenger side of the UPS truck, shooting. On police radio, Santiesteban reported that shots were fired at the officers from the driver’s side of the truck.Judge Krolla said he expects to deal with a few other pre-trial motions Monday and Tuesday and that he expects attorneys to begin choosing jurors for Mateo’s trial some time on Wednesday. Supporters for Jose Mateo listen in court as lawyers argue Florida’s Stand-Your-Ground statute before Judge Ernest A. Kollra on Friday, Aug. 22, 2025. Mateo is one of four Miami-Dade officers charged with manslaughter in the case stemming from the death of UPS driver Frank Ordonez, who was shot by police during a shootout with his kidnappers. full_text: Judge says state can’t stop plea deal. Key Biscayne coach gets 12 years for sex crimes Crime Judge says state can’t stop plea deal. Key Biscayne coach gets 12 years for sex crimes By Charles Rabin and Clara-Sophia Daly Updated August 21, 2025 6:10 PM Miami-Dade Judge Alberto Milian ruled Thursday, Aug. 21, 2025, there would be no trial for Oscar Olea, above, the Key Biscayne gymnastics coach who as a result of a plea deal, will spend 12 years in prison on his sex crime convictions. He was accused of sexually assaulting girls who were students in his program. Carl Juste cjuste@miamiherald.com Despite detailed statements and objections from two sexual assault victims, Miami-Dade Circuit Court Judge Alberto Milian said Thursday there would be no trial for former Key Biscayne gymnastics instructor Oscar Olea, who last week reached a deal with prosecutors to avoid what was likely to be a lengthy and gut-wrenching trial.The judge reached his decision after nearly two hours of discussion and despite state prosecutors asking that the deal be reneged after two of Olea’s three victims said they were dissatisfied with the terms. One victim said she didn’t agree with the plea deal, but despite her disagreement, she deferred to whatever decision the state made, her attorney said.Olea, 40, will spend the next 12 years in prison, followed by a decade of probation. He will also be listed as a registered sex offender, a scar for life that keeps him away from minors and specific distances from gathering spots like parks and schools.“I didn’t take this job because I thought it would be easy,” Milian said just before Olea agreed to the terms of the agreement. “But I conclude this was in fact a meeting of the minds. My heart goes out to the victims. Justice is very imperfect.” Oscar Olea, right, listens as Miami-Dade Judge Alberto Milian explains his plea deal while standing next to his attorneys -- Charlton Stoner, left, and Matthew Ladd, center, inside Courtroom 7-2 at the Richard E. Gerstein Justice Building on Thursday, Aug. 21, 2025, in Miami, Florida. Carl Juste cjuste@miamiherald.com One of Olea’s victims said the former gymnastics instructor stole more than just her virginity and made her a victim - something she never asked for.“That identity was forced on me by someone else’s action, actions that stole something sacred, my virginity, my purity, my innocence,” said 28-year-old A.E., who was 12 when she was assaulted by Olea. “Things I can never get back.”READ MORE: Key Biscayne’s Dark SecretOlea, seated handcuffed in the jury box in an orange jumpsuit, sat silently, often jittery and shaking his legs, as his victims shared horrific stories. He answered Milian’s questions with simple “yes sir” and “no sir” responses. With the plea deal, Olea is now convicted of two counts of lewd and lascivious battery and two counts of unlawful sexual activity with a minor.The agreement stipulates that when Olea leaves prison he will not have access to electronic devices, he won’t be permitted to contact victims or family members and he must stay away from the Village of Key Biscayne until his probation concludes. Though each of the four charges carry a 15-year sentence, state prosecutors said a scoring system they use to determine prison stays would have landed Olea behind bars for 19 years.Before formally accepting the plea, Milian told Olea’s victims they were courageous and created a path forward for future victims of similar crimes. Still, in urging them to accept the plea, he warned them of just how imperfect the legal system can be.“Twelve years is not enough,” he said. “But, sometimes, there is not justice” at all.‘I obeyed out of fear’Olea’s three victims all spoke during the hearing. A.E. told the judge that Olea deserved more than 12 years behind bars. She said he assaulted her when she was 12 and that he stole her virginity and “purity.”“It lives with me. It has touched every single part of who I am,” she said. “I hated myself. I obeyed out of fear.” Oscar Olea, left, is fingerprinted inside Courtroom 7-2 at the Richard E. Gerstein Justice Building on Thursday, Aug. 21, 2025, in Miami, Florida. Miami-Dade Judge Alberto Milian ruled state prosecutors could not renege on Olea’s plea deal of 12 years in prison. Olea’s victims were dissatisfied with the deal. Carl Juste cjuste@miamiherald.com Another of Olea’s victims said, “This man took everything from me... it took me time to realize he brainwashed me.” The victim, who went by the initials E.M., says she wished she’d have spoken out sooner, but she was “completely terrified.”The woman, who is now in her 30s and said she was raped when she was 16, struck a defiant tone after the sentencing: “He has no power on me. I was a victim and now I am a survivor.”READ MORE: ‘Direct insult’: Victim in Key Biscayne gymnastics case demands trialHerald investigation gets police attentionOlea’s sordid history played out mostly in the dark for more than a decade as law enforcement investigations were bungled and parents grappled with how to respond to the belief that their young child had been sexually assaulted.It wasn’t until a 2024 Miami Herald investigation uncovered long-dormant allegations of sexual abuse from three former students, that the story grabbed the public and Key Biscayne Police Department’s attention. The three women, all in their 20s and 30s now, said they were sexually abused by Olea when they were 12, 16 and 16.Charges were never brought in the case involving one woman who spoke Thursday because the statute of limitations had passed. She was a colleague of Olea’s at the Key Biscayne Community Center.One victim said she was sexually assaulted more than 10 times between 2011 and 2012, during private lessons with Olea. Another woman’s mother told the Herald that Olea raped her daughter when she was 17. And a third woman told investigators she was underage and working with Olea at the Key Biscayne Community Center, known as “The Rec,” when they began a sexual relationship that often involved liquor.The Herald investigation also found that more recently, police and the Miami-Dade State Attorney’s Office investigated cases against two young girls ages 4 and 7. But charges were never brought, state prosecutors said, because of inconsistent statements from victims, statements from witnesses that contradicted each other and Olea’s denial of the allegations. In the end, the state said it did not have enough evidence to try the cases despite the police reports.Key Biscayne Police failed to fully investigateThe cases essentially sat stale for over a decade - in part - because the Key Biscayne Police Department failed to act on multiple complaints, including one in 2012 in which a child’s mother brought police love letters between her 14-year-old daughter and Olea. Ocner mocner@miamiherald.com On Thursday in the Miami-Dade criminal courtroom of Judge Alberto Milian, the fate of the Key Biscayne gymnastics coach accused of assaulting two of his students when they were children will be decided.Last week, Oscar Olea, now 40, and the Miami-Dade State Attorney’s Office signed a plea deal — which stipulated that Olea would spend 12 years in prison, followed by a decade of probation. full_text: Dresden: Man arrested after tram knife attack on US citizen CrimeGermanyDresden: Man arrested after tram knife attack on US citizenMark Hallam08/26/2025August 26, 2025A 21-year-old Syrian citizen is in investigative custody in Dresden after a young American man was stabbed in the face on a tram over the weekend in the eastern German city. New information may link him to the attack.https://p.dw.com/p/4zXfyThe attack took place just after midnight on Sunday in the city in Saxony (file photo of Dresden police officer from 2024)Image: Robert Michael/dpa/picture allianceAdvertisementDresden police and prosecutors said on Tuesday that they had arrested a 21-year-old Syrian in connection with a knife attack on a late-night tram in the city over the weekend. He was detained in the early hours of Tuesday, police said, and was put in investigative custody on suspicion of grievous bodily harm, among other offenses. The man in question had already been detained once before and was released soon after the incident, with no initial indication of him being directly involved in injuring a young American. But investigators said new information might implicate him more directly. Police said in a press release that after further investigation there was now reasonable grounds to suspect that he was involved in the knife attack against the 20-year-old American and also himself injured the victim with a dangerous object. Tuesday's statement made no direct mention of the second suspect, originally believed to be the prime culprit behind the injuries sustained by the American man. As of Monday afternoon, authorities in the eastern German state of Saxony were still seeking him and had appealed for help from potential witnesses. US Embassy in Berlin calls for swift, severe punishment The victim was wounded after stepping in to try to protect another female passenger on the tram who was being harassed, according to police. The US Embassy in Berlin condemned the brutal attack in a statement online, and called on German authorities to swiftly bring the perpetrators to justice and punish them to the fullest extent permitted by law. The victim was hospitalized with lacerations to the face but police said the injuries were not life-threatening. Police and prosecutors said that their investigations were ongoing and that as a result of this they could not yet provide further details. full_text: Dresden tram stabbing: Police appeal for witnesses CrimeGermanyDresden tram stabbing: Police appeal for witnessesKieran Burke08/25/2025August 25, 2025A US citizen was stabbed when he tried to stop two men from harassing female passengers on a tram, according to the police, who are now searching for any clues.https://p.dw.com/p/4zSWHAuthorities have appealed for witnesses to come forward following the stabbing incident in the eastern city of Dresden (file photo)Image: Tino Plunert/dpa/picture allianceAdvertisementPolice in the eastern German city of Dresden have appealed for witnesses to come forward after a stabbing incident that took place on a tram in the early hours of Sunday morning. What Dresden police have said about the stabbing Police said that an altercation took place involving three people on the Gorbitz-bound tram at the the Neustädter Markt stop early Sunday at 00:25 local time (2225 UTC/GMT late Saturday). The police apprehended a 21-year-old Syrian national but have yet to capture an unidentified man wanted for grievous bodily harm, among other things. US daily tabloid The New York Post published pictures appearing to show the interior of the blood-spattered tram. Police confirmed that the man who had been detained had since been released as the search for the other suspect continued. full_text: US court throws out massive fraud penalty against Trump Law and JusticeUnited States of AmericaUS court throws out massive fraud penalty against TrumpRoshni Majumdar with AP, Reuters08/21/2025August 21, 2025A New York appeals court has ruled that US President Donald Trump will not be required to pay a $515 million (around €443 million) civil fraud penalty, eliminating one of his biggest financial liabilities.https://p.dw.com/p/4zKrVThe latest ruling only applies to financial penalties levied against Trump and his executivesImage: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFPAdvertisementA US court on Thursday threw out the half-billion-dollar penalty in the civil fraudcase against President Donald Trump and his company. But a panel of five judges upheld other punishments, including a lower court's finding that Trump and Trump Organization executives engaged in fraud. New York Attorney General Letitia James had sued Trump in 2022, alleging he falsely altered his net worth on key financial statements to receive tax and insurance benefits. The lawsuit made James one of Trump's most prominent adversaries. A New York judge Arthur Engoron last year ordered Trump to pay nearly $355 million in penalties after holding him liable for fraud. With interest, that sum topped $515 million. If including additional penalties levied on Trump's eldest sons, Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump, the total balloons to more than $527 million as of Thursday. Judges say penalty 'excessive' but disagree over merits of lawsuit The court agreed to eliminate the penalty that came with the verdict, writing that the order which directs that defendants pay nearly half a billion dollars to the State of New York, is an excessive fine that violates the Eighth Amendment of the United States Constitution. But the panel remained sharply divided on the merits of the lawsuit and Engoron's fraud finding. Two judges wrote that they felt New York Attorney General Letitia James' lawsuit against Trump and his companies was justifiable and that she had proven her case, even with the penalty being too severe. Another judge wrote that James exceeded her legal authority in bringing the suit, saying that if any of Trump's lenders felt cheated, they could have sued him themselves, and none did. One judge wrote that Engoron was wrong to rule, before the trial began, that the attorney general had proved Trump engaged in fraud. Trump claims 'total victory' after NY appeals court decision Trump and his sons painted the ruling as a win, with Trump posting to Truth Social that: TOTAL VICTORY in the FAKE New York State Attorney General Letitia James Case! I greatly respect the fact that the Court had the Courage to throw out this unlawful and disgraceful Decision that was hurting Business all throughout New York State. Eric Trump, the president's son, wrote to X: Total victory in the sham NY Attorney General case!!! After 5 years of hell, justice prevailed! Court ruling upholds other punishments The court in the same ruling said that other non-monetary sanctions imposed by Arthur Engoron on Trump, the Trump Organization, and other defendants were well crafted to curb defendants’ business culture. Judges Peter Moulten and Dianne Renwick, who wrote the principal opinion, said that the trial record supports the lower court’s finding that Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump, possessed the requisite intent to defraud, in addition to top executives Allen Weisselberg and Jeffrey McConney, according to The Hill. full_text: Starvation is a war crime, but will justice ever be done? ConflictsPalestinian TerritoriesStarvation is a war crime, but will justice ever be done?Cathrin Schaer08/15/2025August 15, 2025Experts say that food is increasingly being used as a weapon in conflicts in places like Sudan, Syria and Gaza. But there's never been a war crimes case about it in an international court. That may soon change.https://p.dw.com/p/4z3Y1Aid agencies and human rights organizations say Israel is deliberately starving civilians in Gaza, a charge Israel deniesImage: Ahmed Jihad Ibrahim Al-arini/Anadolu/picture allianceAdvertisementCalls to prosecute the war crime of starvation are becoming louder and more frequent. [Famine] is a weapon of war being wielded across the globe at the moment. But this has to stop, it's against international humanitarian law, Shayna Lewis, senior adviser on Sudan for the US-based group PAEMA (Preventing and Ending Mass Atrocities) told DW recently. She was talking about the Sudanese city of El Fasher, which has been under siege for a year now and where food is running out for around 30,000 people trapped there. It is a crime internationally and it needs to be prosecuted as such, Lewis argued. Human rights groups, including Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, have said similar about Israel's blockade of aid and food into the Gaza Strip. Israel is starving Gaza. It's genocide. It's a crime against humanity. It's a war crime, Michael Fakhri, the United Nations' special rapporteur on the right to food, told UK newspaper the Guardian last week. The western Sudanese city of El Fasher has been under siege for almost a year. Around 300,000 inhabitants are at risk of famine.Image: UNICEF/Xinhua/picture alliance Food as a weapon of war Experts say that part of the reason there are now more calls to prosecute starvation of civilians as a war crime, is that there is more famine being caused by conflict. Over the first decade of this century, there was very little famine, researchers at the World Peace Foundation, or WPF, wrote in a 2022 collection of essays, Accountability for Starvation. But more recently that has changed. This is an ancient phenomenon, warring parties have been using it for centuries, Rebecca Bakos Blumenthal, a legal adviser with the Starvation Accountability project run by Netherlands-based law foundation, Global Rights Compliance, or GRC, says. After 2015, this kind of tactic has re-emerged, she noted. Syria's ousted dictator Bashar Assad's strategy of 'Besiege, starve, force to surrender' saw Yarmouk, Damascus, sealed off in 2013 with 18,000 civilians trapped thereImage: UNRWA via AP/picture alliance Over the past decade, there have been conflict-related famines in Nigeria, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Syria and Yemen. Food security experts suggest Russian attacks on Ukraine's agricultural sector could also be seen as criminal attempts to weaponize food. Basically there's just more of this war crime happening again, they argue. Even while global food security is improving, the incidence of famines is increasing, Alex de Waal, a professor at Tufts University in the US and head of the WPF's research into mass starvation, wrote last week. This tells us that the global food security is more volatile and unequal. That's consistent with hunger being used as a weapon. The deliberate withholding of food or other essentials needed for civilians' survival is categorized as a war crime by many nations as well as in various iterations of international law, including the Geneva Conventions and the Rome Statute (which is applied by the International Criminal Court, or ICC). But so far, those who wield that weapon have never been brought to trial: The war crime of starvation has never been prosecuted in an international court on its own, only as a part of around 20 other war crimes cases. And just because civilians are going hungry in a conflict, doesn't mean a crime was committed. One of the issues in law is the question of intent, de Waal told DW. The war crime of starvation requires that the perpetrator is acting with intent. Starvation was not always classified as a war crime: Nazi Germany's siege of Leningrad, which resulted in hundreds of thousands dying from starvation between 1941 and 1942, was considered a legal tacticImage: akg-images/picture alliance Starvation happens over the longer term, de Waal points out, and some legal scholars have argued it must be proven that a perpetrator intended to starve people from the very beginning of, for example, a siege or blockade. But most legal experts believe there could also be indirect intent, de Waal explains. That is, it's clear that starvation will occur in the normal course of events, and the perpetrator knows that, they've had opportunities to prevent it, but didn't do so. Another issue for any legal case involving starvation is the lack of precedent, and which international or national courts have jurisdiction over the alleged war criminals. Changing views on starvation as war crime Up until a couple of years ago, starvation was often seen as a developmental or humanitarian issue, GRC's Blumenthal explains. But now there is more attention being paid to its criminal aspects. I've worked on this issue for quite a few years now and these things do move slowly, concedes Blumenthal, who's been looking at the topic since 2020. But I do think the needle is moving and there have been some consequential steps taken over the past 10 years. Starvation as a war crime has occasionally been in national courts: In Croatia in 1997, officers of the former Yugoslav People’s Army were tried in absentia for the siege of the city of ZadarImage: Gepa/AP Photo/picture alliance In 2018, the UN Security Council unanimously passed Resolution 2417, condemning the starving of civilians as a method of warfare. In 2019, changes were made to the Rome Statute, making starvation a war crime in non-international armed conflicts too, rather than just international. There have also been UN commissions of inquiry on conflicts in South Sudan and Ethiopia-Tigray specifically focusing on the topic of starvation as a war crime, Blumenthal points out. We're seeing a lot more international and local organizations, together with accountability mechanisms, calling this out and certain striking examples, like the case of Gaza today, have really amplified awareness around the crime as well, she notes. In fact, the ICC warrants issued against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Israeli defense minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024, which specifically mention the war crime of starvation, are a historic milestone, Blumenthal notes. It's the first time that international warrants have been issued for starvation as a stand-alone crime. The ICC also has an open investigation into Sudan going, she adds. The issue has undoubtedly gained more attention over the last 10 years, de Waal confirms. The legal frameworks are all in place. What's lacking is the political will to act. In Gaza, desperation grows as food supplies dwindleTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Will perpetrators of starvation ever end up in court? There are still jurisdictional challenges, de Waal told DW. But I am confident that there are many cases for which conviction is possible. It just requires getting the accused in court. Blumenthal agrees. There are misconceptions around this and so many people think [starvation] is an inevitable part of war, she says. But during our in-depth investigations, it's surprising how quickly it becomes clear that actually these patterns are very stark and in many situations, you can discern a deliberate strategy. Blumenthal is cautiously optimistic that one day soon those who deliberately starve civilians will face justice. That is certainly the hope, she concludes. That's what we are all working towards. But most legal experts believe there could also be indirect intent, de Waal explains. That is, it's clear that starvation will occur in the normal course of events, and the perpetrator knows that, they've had opportunities to prevent it, but didn't do so. Another issue for any legal case involving starvation is the lack of precedent, and which international or national courts have jurisdiction over the alleged war criminals. Changing views on starvation as war crime Up until a couple of years ago, starvation was often seen as a developmental or humanitarian issue, GRC's Blumenthal explains. But now there is more attention being paid to its criminal aspects. I've worked on this issue for quite a few years now and these things do move slowly, concedes Blumenthal, who's been looking at the topic since 2020. But I do think the needle is moving and there have been some consequential steps taken over the past 10 years. Starvation as a war crime has occasionally been in national courts: In Croatia in 1997, officers of the former Yugoslav People’s Army were tried in absentia for the siege of the city of ZadarImage: Gepa/AP Photo/picture alliance In 2018, the UN Security Council unanimously passed Resolution 2417, condemning the starving of civilians as a method of warfare. In 2019, changes were made to the Rome Statute, making starvation a war crime in non-international armed conflicts too, rather than just international. There have also been UN commissions of inquiry on conflicts in South Sudan and Ethiopia-Tigray specifically focusing on the topic of starvation as a war crime, Blumenthal points out. We're seeing a lot more international and local organizations, together with accountability mechanisms, calling this out and certain striking examples, like the case of Gaza today, have really amplified awareness around the crime as well, she notes. In fact, the ICC warrants issued against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Israeli defense minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024, which specifically mention the war crime of starvation, are a historic milestone, Blumenthal notes. It's the first time that international warrants have been issued for starvation as a stand-alone crime. The ICC also has an open investigation into Sudan going, she adds. The issue has undoubtedly gained more attention over the last 10 years, de Waal confirms. The legal frameworks are all in place. What's lacking is the political will to act. In Gaza, desperation grows as food supplies dwindleTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Will perpetrators of starvation ever end up in court? There are still jurisdictional challenges, de Waal told DW. But I am confident that there are many cases for which conviction is possible. It just requires getting the accused in court. Blumenthal agrees. There are misconceptions around this and so many people think [starvation] is an inevitable part of war, she says. But during our in-depth investigations, it's surprising how quickly it becomes clear that actually these patterns are very stark and in many situations, you can discern a deliberate strategy. Blumenthal is cautiously optimistic that one day soon those who deliberately starve civilians will face justice. That is certainly the hope, she concludes. That's what we are all working towards. who: Jonah Kariuki; Kariuki; Albert Ojwang; Thomas Mukoya/; Tensions; Gen Z-led; Andrew Kasuku/AP Photo; William Ruto; Ndungi Githuku; Kongamano La Mapinduzi; Simon Maina/AFP/Getty Images

full_text: What you need to know about Kenyan protester's shooting PoliticsKenyaWhat you need to know about Kenyan protester's shootingMartina Schwikowski06/18/2025June 18, 2025The shooting in one of Nairobi's busiest streets outraged many Kenyans who have long witnessed officers abusing protesters and bystanders. Human rights groups are concerned about the rising lawlessness in Kenya.https://p.dw.com/p/4w8BuYoung Kenyans have borne the brunt of brutality by police forces in large cities like NairobiImage: Brian Inganga/AP/picture allianceAdvertisementWhat happened? In Nairobi's business district, small groups of protesters gathered on Tuesday, initially peacefully, to call for an end to police brutality. But according to media reports, they were quickly attacked by hundreds of men on motorbikes armed with makeshift weapons, known in Kenya as goons. Nairobi: Police, protesters clash in second week of unrestTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Police vehicles and officers appeared as vendors hastily packed up their stalls. One of the officers pointed his gun in the direction of protesters, then ran with a colleague to a vendor named Jonah Kariuki. The officers pushed the man. As he is shoved and is moving away, Kariuki glances back. The officer raises his weapon and shoots 22-year-old Kariuki at close range in the head — who crumples to the sidewalk. After the shooting, the officer and his colleague walk away. Police's reaction to the shooting Police did not directly deny any cooperation with the armed goons, releasing a statement saying it does not condone such unlawful groupings. Police also said the officer who shot Kariuki in the head using an anti-riot shotgun had been arrested. Activists called for the officer to be charged. The judiciary in a statement on Wednesday said it was committed to uphold justice in all cases, including those involving alleged police brutality. Nairobi: Pro-government counter-protesters clash with a protester during a protest over the death of Kenyan blogger Albert Ojwang in police custodyImage: Thomas Mukoya/REUTERS A wave of protests Tensions were already high in the East African country as it marks a year since massive Gen Z-led protests over the economy. Kenyan government's latest finance bill avoided the tax hikes that sparked weeks of protests in mid-2024. Rights groups say over 60 people were killed and dozens more were illegally detained by security forces in the aftermath. The protests peaked when thousands stormed parliament on June 25, 2024 when lawmakers debated the unpopular finance bill. The bill is now expected to take effect on July 1, 2025. But demonstrations picked up again over the death of 31-year-old teacher and blogger Albert Ojwang, who died in police custody earlier this month. Protesters want a senior officer they blame for the death to resign. A protester scuffles with police during the recent protests in downtown NairobiImage: Andrew Kasuku/AP Photo/picture alliance History of state violence Kenya has a history of politicians using armed mobs. Earlier this year, President William Ruto was accused of paying goons to follow his cavalcade around a tour of Nairobi to prevent protests. Ruto adamantly denied paying any mobs after the tour was cut short amid widespread violence and robberies against bystanders. Rights groups concerned We are turning into a lawless country, Ndungi Githuku, of civil rights group Kongamano La Mapinduzi, told AFP at Tuesday's protest. We see hundreds of paid goons, with whips and weapons, crude weapons, coming to brutalize our people. Despite reforms to improve the relationship between police and citizens, human rights activists say police have not managed to transform their image from an authoritarian force to one that serves Kenyan citizens within a democracy.The wave of protestes of young Kenyans in Nairobi's streets against police brutality continues Image: Simon Maina/AFP/Getty Images Edited by: Cai Nebe Martina Schwikowski Author for the Africa deskSend us your feedbackYour feedbackAdvertisement
