full_text: Dezi Freeman: the church-going, gun-owning bushman on the loose The search for Dezi Freeman continues as Porepunkah reckons with sovereign citizen ideologyBy Ben Butler, Danny Tran, Kate Ashton and Danielle BonicaTopic:CrimeFri 29 AugFriday 29 AugustFri 29 Aug 2025 at 9:19pmA path leading to Mount Buffalo National Park, which is located next to Porepunkah. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)In short:People who know alleged police killer Dezi Freeman say he is a religious man who also possesses a frightening firearms arsenal.Mr Freeman has been on the run since Tuesday after he allegedly shot dead two police officers and injured a third at a Porepunkah property.What's next?Locals in the nearby tourist town of Bright have shared mixed reactions to the alleged beliefs of Mr Freeman.abc.net.au/news/dezi-freeman-sovereign-citizen-porepunkah/105711310Link copiedShareShare articleIt was at the end of a track — surrounded by cold, dense bushland rising above a small Victorian town — where Dezi Freeman's years of anger and anti-government conspiracy theories boiled over.To quote his local priest, who was aware of some of his beliefs after seeing him at church nearly every Sunday, Mr Freeman absolutely cracked .Allegedly armed with a homemade shotgun and other firearms, Mr Freeman is suspected to have shot dead police officers Neal Thompson and Vadim De Waart — and wounded a third — as they were serving a warrant at the Porepunkah property in the state's alpine region on Tuesday, sparking an unprecedented manhunt.As 450 police officers scour rugged and now snow-covered terrain for the experienced bushman, Mr Freeman's actions have revealed a community fraying over anti-authoritarian ideology taken to its unthinkable extreme.The prolonged search has prompted speculation that the heavily armed fugitive might not get out of the bush alive.Dezi Bird Freeman allegedly shot dead police officers Neal Thompson and Vadim De Waart, prompting a manhunt. (Supplied) After doing what he's done already, I'd say he will … try and make himself a martyr, one former special operations police officer tells the ABC.However this story might end, Mr Freeman's alleged attack on police has put the focus on a set of fractured beliefs festering not only in the town of Porepunkah, but in communities like it across the country.A church-going, obsessive, anti-authoritarianAccording to those who know him, Mr Freeman is a religious man who also possesses a frightening firearms arsenal.He regularly took his kids fishing and taught friends how to dive, but posted online that the only good cop is a dead cop and urged the incineration of police, labelling them the new Gestapo .With his family, he attended mass regularly at a Catholic church, Our Lady of the Snows, perched on a hillside on the outskirts of the nearby tourist town of Bright.Mr Freeman regularly attended mass at a Catholic church in Bright. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)The local priest, Father Tony Shallue, says that after a statue at the church was vandalised, Mr Freeman was the one who helped to fix it. I knew he was a bit anti-authority, but a lot of people are, says Fr Shallue. But I've never encountered him as someone who would do that. It's a shock. He's thinking of cancelling mass on Sunday, as you've got to think of people's safety .Most in the regional community share Fr Shallue's horror over the alleged murder of two serving police officers.Many residents of the small town of Porepunkah are shocked by this week's fatalities. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)But Mr Freeman's ideology was not formed in a vacuum.His views — though not his alleged actions — continue to be supported by some in the community who spoke to the ABC, demonstrating the reach of sovereign citizen beliefs in society, even in a tiny town like Porepunkah.At home in the High CountryFor Mr Freeman, who was previously known as Desmond Filby, the dense hills, mountains and valleys surrounding Porepunkah are home.According to an old friend who has known him for decades, Mr Freeman struggled to hold down a job and has been on a disability pension since the early 2000s.He moved around the region, and previously lived at one address down the end of Buffalo Creek Road in nearby Myrtleford.Locals are keen to point out that the address is just over a ridge through the Mt Buffalo National Park from Porepunkah — a tough trek for most people but an easy walk for an experienced bushman like Mr Freeman.The road becomes dirt and ends at a sign proclaiming no shooting , telling would-be visitors that beyond the open gate is private property.A no shooting and private property sign marks the end of the road nearby Mr Freeman's previous address. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)This area is littered with similar signs warning off unauthorised visitors.Mr Freeman would tear down signs like these, according to former neighbour Loretta Quinn.She says he would fly his drone over her land constantly, cut locks off her gates and generally treat her property like his extended playground .A history of disputes with neighbours and local authoritiesMr Freeman believed he had a right to be on her property and would not accept that it was not public land, she says.The dispute widened to include the local council, according to documents he filed with the Victorian Supreme Court last year.It eventually got so out of hand Ms Quinn contacted police and took out an intervention order.She says that didn't really work, with his extreme views apparently challenging for police to handle.Dezi Freeman was previously seen wearing a body camera during an alleged argument about property boundaries. (Supplied)He would also constantly be filming — always wearing a body camera, she says — and as his neighbour, she always felt watched.When the news broke that he was accused of shooting two police officers, Ms Quinn felt a familiar sense of panic. I was terrified of him, she says.But not everyone was.Mr Freeman had friends and supportersProtected from the rain by a well-used Drizabone and a bushman's hat, Stephen Mallett is an ex-bikie who knows Mr Freeman from a Facebook group dedicated to preparing for the apocalypse.Mr Mallett makes and sells wooden knives in a local shop at Bright, which is how the ABC managed to get in touch.Walking alongside his two wolfhounds, Georgie Whitesocks and Tucker Goldenheart, Mr Mallett also wants to make it clear he does not personally identify as a sovereign citizen — a term he doesn't like.Stephen Mallett knew Mr Freeman from a Facebook group dedicated to apocalypse preparation. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica) 'Sovereign citizen', they're using that as a name now to vilify people, he says.While it is difficult to define the exact views held by people who associate with sovereign citizen beliefs, there is a tendency to reject widely accepted laws and government power.No matter how he identifies, Mr Mallett admits he has a similar way of thinking to people like Mr Freeman. The nutters are going to jump on this, but a nutter he wasn't, he says.Previous run-ins with local policeFrom the outset, Mr Mallett says Mr Freeman did the wrong thing by allegedly killing two officers. But he claims Mr Freeman is the victim of a long campaign of persecution at the hands of Victoria Police. They were going for him, for sure, he says.The examples Mr Mallett gives for Mr Freeman's persecution include his arrest outside the Myrtleford courthouse during a 2021 demonstration following a failed private prosecution of then-premier Daniel Andrews for treason and fraud.Mr Mallett says Mr Freeman is the victim of a long campaign of persecution at the hands of Victoria Police. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)In documents filed with the court, a Bright chiropractor who brought the charges said that Mr Andrews had committed treason by removing the queen's name from official documents and replacing it with the state of Victoria.The court hearing descended into chaos with participants, who joined by video link, showing pictures of their chickens and doctored images of Mr Andrews as a dictator, according to multiple media reports.According to those who know Mr Freeman, the episode was a key moment that solidified his attitude towards police and the authority of the state.It was followed by police suspending Mr Freeman's drivers license after he was stopped for speeding and refused to take a drug test, leading to the loss of two of his cars, Mr Mallett says.Last year, the suspected killer complained to the Supreme Court that he had his firearms licence cancelled and lost membership to his gun club.Mr Mallett also does not like police, nor does he believe in select hate crime laws.Police blocked off Rayner Lane in Porepunkah near the property where the alleged shooting of two police officers took place. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)He loathes that police, as he puts it, can dress in black with their jackboots and put roadblocks on the side of the road and put dogs on people, while a physical gesture like a Nazi salute is a crime.Friend recalls Mr Freeman's 'arsenal' of weaponsWhile 10 officers arrived at his Porepunkah home on Tuesday, none were part of the heavily armed special operations group.Instead, they were there to execute a search warrant over alleged historical child sex offences.But Mr Freeman was armed. He had been for years, even after losing his gun licence.Mick, who requested to be identified only by his first name, is an old friend of Mr Freeman's who pulls off the highway to talk to the ABC.He says he was once shown part of Mr Freeman's arsenal of weapons.Mick says he is an old friend of Mr Freeman's and has previously been inside his home. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica) He had high-powered rifles and he had military rifles, he says. He has got stuff that you wouldn't even dream about. I saw it with my own eyes, years ago. Mick says Mr Freeman had a firing range up in the bush where he would practise target shooting. He was a bloody good shot, Mick says. Every shot counts. 'Modern-day Rambo' that won't surrender, friend saysOn Thursday, police called for Mr Freeman's surrender, and re-iterated that the situation could be managed safely.But Mick also says he does not believe Mr Freeman will surrender.He tells the ABC that Mr Freeman would sometimes disappear into the bush for a couple of days at a time and could carry two freshly killed deer on his back. He's a modern-day Rambo, he says. There's not a chance of getting him alive. Mick told the ABC that Mr Freeman would sometimes disappear into the bush for days at a time. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)Mr Freeman's former neighbour, Ms Quinn, agrees. I think it'll be a Ned Kelly scene, she says I just hope no-one else gets hurt now. I don't know how they're going to stop him. As the former police special operations officer tells the ABC, in the dense bushland and freezing conditions, Mr Freeman has the home ground advantage .But he says police are trained for this scenario and they're working bloody hard .Quiet towns overwhelmed by police presenceWhile the search for Mr Freeman continues, the police presence on the roads around Bright and Porepunkah is overwhelming.Convoys of police cars travel at speed down the mountain roads while overhead helicopters circle the national park.Porepunkah, home to just over 1,000 people, is eerily quiet when the ABC visits. At one point, the only people on the streets are a couple walking their dogs and a TV crew.But Porepunkah and Bright make up a small community where even people who appear to be outsiders are connected.A police staging area just outside of Porepunkah was set up as part of the search operation for Dezi Freeman. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)Mr Freeman's wife, Mali, played at local venues as part of a duo with another High Country musician. She was arrested and interviewed by police before being released without charge on Thursday night.And the wife of the Bright chiropractor who brought treason charges against the former premier — prompting the demonstration for which Mr Freeman was subsequently arrested — works at a winery in Porepunkah from where Victoria Police is staging its search.Police search the talk of neighbouring town BrightMeanwhile, Bright is abuzz with talk of the hunt for Mr Freeman. Police are everywhere. Police cars whiz by every few minutes and hungry officers recharge in the cafes and bakeries.A hiker speaks into his phone, loudly telling whoever is on the other end — and anyone else within earshot — that he doesn't think police will be able to find Mr Freeman.There remains a heavy police presence in the nearby tourist town of Bright. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)In one shop, the man behind the counter tells the ABC how he himself has explored the mines that are scattered across the mountainside.You can go in as deep as 200 metres and it's a toasty 20 degrees inside, he says — very different from the bitter single-digit temperatures outside at night.But underneath the surface, the shootings have reopened divisions in the community between people whose families have lived here for generations and those who have moved here more recently to get away from the mainstream.In the local Bright Facebook group, a furious debate has erupted after one local posted: Sorry, Sovereign Citizens aren't welcome here. A local Bright Facebook group has garnered mixed views about Mr Freeman and his political beliefs. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)The 141-post thread soon devolved into free-flowing insults, as people who sympathise with some of Mr Freeman's political beliefs clashed with those who do not.Fr Shallue hadn't heard of sovereign citizens before the shootings, but he says he now understands it as a terrible aspect of our society. People think this stuff happens in the city, but you've got some pretty weird segments of society gathering in the country, he says. I would say the sad thing is these sort of groups just feed into people's pre-existing problems, he says. They just feed the paranoia. It's so disturbing. as it happenedTopic:PoliceFri 29 AugFriday 29 AugustFri 29 Aug 2025 at 7:26pmSkip to timelineabc.net.au/news/dezi-freeman-search-enters-fifth-day-porepunkah/105713972Link copiedShareShare articleVictorian police arrested a 61-year-old man on Saturday after executing a search warrant at a house in Bright, about six kilometres from Porepunkah, where police allege Dezi Freeman shot and killed two police officers on Tuesday.Officers are yet to reveal whether the arrest is linked to the search for Mr Freeman, 56, who is still on the loose despite an extensive police manhunt that has continued for five days.More than 450 state police officers, as well as Australian Federal Police special operators, are involved in the overall investigation.Also on Saturday, officers descended on properties and bushland near Myrtleford, about 30 kilometres from Porepunkah, including Victoria Police's BearCat tactical vehicle.Take a look back at how the day's events unfolded in our live blog below.Key EventsPolice arrest 61-year-old man in BrightSat 30 AugSat 30 AugSat 30 Aug 2025 at 6:09amPolice descend on properties and bushland near MyrtlefordSat 30 AugSat 30 AugSat 30 Aug 2025 at 5:49amPolice relocate search headquarters to OvensSat 30 AugSat 30 AugSat 30 Aug 2025 at 5:20amShow all key eventsLive updatesLatestOldestSat, 7:33amSat 30 Aug 2025 at 7:33amThanks for joining our live coverageABy Andrew ThorpeWe're going to close our live blog here, as it doesn't look like there'll be any more information from police this evening regarding the arrest of a 61-year-old man in Bright or the increased police activity in Myrtleford.If that should change, we'll try to be the first to let you know.To recap, police say there have been several reported sightings of alleged gunman Dezi Freeman, 56, since he went on the run on Tuesday in dense bushland near Porepunkah, though none of these sightings have been confirmed.Dezi Freeman is accused of killing two police officers at Porepunkah on Tuesday. (Supplied)Victoria's police commissioner says police will not stop their search for Freeman — who is accused of gunning down two police officers — until he is found, and anyone helping him evade capture will face criminal charges.People living in Porepunkah and nearby areas have been warned not to approach Freeman, who is believed to be heavily armed, and to stay inside until he is taken into custody.To stay up to date, you can download the ABC News app and subscribe to our range of news alerts for the latest updates.ReactReactCopy linkKey EventSat, 6:09amSat 30 Aug 2025 at 6:09amPolice arrest 61-year-old man in BrightMBy Melissa BrownThe ABC has learnt that police have arrested a man in Bright, just outside Porepunkah.Police say it follows the execution of a search warrant yesterday afternoon, during which guns and cannabis were seized from a home in the area.The arrestee, a 61-year-old man, is still being interviewed by police.When asked whether the arrest was related to the search for Dezi Freeman, 56, a police spokesperson said that will form part of the line of enquiry .She would not comment on the police activity taking place in Clemens Lane, Myrtleford.ReactReactCopy linkKey EventSat, 5:49amSat 30 Aug 2025 at 5:49amPolice descend on properties and bushland near MyrtlefordMBy Melissa BrownA large convoy of police vehicles has driven to Clemens Lane in Myrtleford.It's 30 kilometres by road from the Porepunkah property where police say Dezi Freeman shot and killed the two officers.(ABC News)The BearCat led the convoy this afternoon.Lynne lives along Clemens Lane, and says the whole ordeal is upsetting. They're doing their job, and I hope to God they can get it finished soon, she saysClemens Lane. (ABC News)Another local, Peter, says his wife is feeling uneasy, but he's just trying to get on with his day.He says the local bushland is rugged but can easily be traversed if you're fit and have local knowledge. If you were to go out the other side [of the bushland] into the Buffalo River side, it's probably a nine-hour walk and you come out into Nug Nug Reserve. He could be anywhere. Victoria Police's BearCat. (ABC News)ReactReactCopy linkSat, 5:42amSat 30 Aug 2025 at 5:42amFlags at half-mast in BrightMBy Melissa BrownThe nearest town to Porepunkah is Bright.Despite police urging travellers to stay away from the region because of the search, many people have proceeded with plans to head to Victoria's ski fields after heavy overnight dumps of snow.The streets are busy with travellers stopping in at the town to pick up supplies and snow chains for their car tyres which are needed to reach the ski resorts on Mount Hotham and Falls Creek.Many of them would have passed the Bright Memorial Clock Tower where flags are flying at half-mast as a sign of respect for slain police officers Neal Thompson and Vadim De Waart.Nearby a church in Bright urges the community to think of those taking part in the search for Dezi Freeman.Bright Memorial Clock Tower (ABC News)(ABC News)ReactReactCopy linkKey EventSat, 5:20amSat 30 Aug 2025 at 5:20amPolice relocate search headquarters to OvensMBy Melissa BrownVictoria Police has just issued a statement saying it's relocating its forward command post from Feathertop Winery just outside Porepunkah to a government office in the town of Ovens, about 12 kilometres away. The new site is a fit-for-purpose facility and will best support Victoria Police's operational activity moving forward, the statement says. We would like to reassure the community that police are not leaving the area. Police move out of the Feathertop Winery. (ABC News)ReactReactCopy linkKey EventSat, 5:05amSat 30 Aug 2025 at 5:05amKing River flood warning issued for middle of search areaABy Andrew ThorpeA severe weather warning covering much of Victoria's north-east has been cancelled, but it's been replaced by a minor flood warning for the King River at the Docker Road Bridge, about 20 kilometres south of Wangaratta.The river is currently at 2.61m and rising, according to the Vic Emergency website, and could peak at around 3.70m on Saturday night.The flood warning area (in yellow on the map below) essentially splits the Dangerous Person warning area (in blue) right up the middle — but given the minor nature of the potential flooding and Freeman's reported familiarity with the terrain, there's no reason to think this will help flush the alleged gunman out (if he's even near the river in the first place).The Vic Emergency map as of 2:52pm on Saturday. (ABC News)The police manhunt isn't deterring those chasing one last ski trip. (ABC News)This skier tells the ABC he's comforted by the large police presence. (ABC News)This skier says he isn't worried about being in any danger, believing the large police presence will help protect the community. We just follow the rules and we'll be safe, he says. full_text: Vengeful killer who shot dead innocent man in his own bedroom jailed Peter Nguyen-Ha sentenced to 22 years for murdering Ralph Matthews Cox in LandsdaleDBy David WeberTopic:CourtsFri 29 AugFriday 29 AugustFri 29 Aug 2025 at 9:14amPeter Nguyen-Ha, 34, was convicted of murdering Ralph Matthews Cox following a jury trial. (Supplied: Anne Barnetson)In short:Peter Nguyen-Ha has been sentenced to at least 22 years' jail after he shot dead Ralph Matthews Cox in his Landsdale home.The 35-year old had been on parole for drug offences and had fired at the home in an attempt to scare Anthony Prior, who had been living at the property.Nguyen-Ha was also sentenced over his involvement in three other shootings.abc.net.au/news/peter-nguyen-ha-gets-22-years-for-murdering-ralph-matthews-cox/105686824Link copiedShareShare articleA man who fired a shotgun through a bedroom window in suburban Perth, killing an innocent man, has been jailed by a Perth court for a minimum of 22 years.Peter Nguyen-Ha, 35, was on parole for drug offences when he shot Ralph Matthews Cox in his Landsdale house in January 2022, in an apparent attempt to scare someone who stole money from him.But Supreme Court Judge Bruno Fiannaca said the abhorrent vigilante behaviour had resulted in the death of an innocent man who had no involvement with Nguyen-Ha. Revenge was at the heart of your criminal purpose, Justice Fiannaca told him.'Kind, gentle' victimHe said Mr Matthews Cox was kind, generous and gentle , and his loss had been profound for his family.In finding Nguyen-Ha guilty, Justice Fiannaca rejected his claim that Matthew Gempton, who was with him at the time, was the real killer.Ralph Matthews Cox was described by the judge as a kind, generous and gentle man. (Facebook)As the judge read this out, Nguyen-Ha sat in the dock, looking down and shaking his head.The judge said his unwillingness to admit he was the shooter was a chilling demonstration of callousness .Bullet holes were left in the bedroom window of the Landsdale house after the shooting. (Supplied: Supreme Court of Western Australia)He said children were in the Landsdale house when the killing occurred.Nguyen-Ha bore considerable animosity towards Anthony Prior, who had been living at Mr Matthews Cox's home, and who had stolen tens of thousands of dollars from him in a staged drug deal.Multiple shootingsThe Landsdale incident was the last in a series of shootings which Nguyen-Ha was involved in during his failed attempts to find Mr Prior.Earlier in January, Nguyen-Ha fired a rifle at a home in Girrawheen, and was with a man who fired a shotgun at the same house in a second incident, and also at a home in Wanneroo.Forensics officers scour the scene after the shooting death of Ralph Matthews Cox. (ABC News)Nguyen-Ha was found guilty of four charges of doing an act to endanger life in relation to those incidents.His sentences for those crimes will be served concurrently with his minimum 22 years for murder.The court heard that at the time of the shootings, Nguyen-Ha was on parole after serving a prison sentence for drug offences.Bullet holes were left in the bedroom window of the house where Ralph Matthews Cox was fatally shot. (Supplied: Supreme Court of Western Australia)He had an extensive criminal record, including aggravated burglary, and had spent much of his adulthood in custody. It has been a wasted life, Justice Fiannaca said, and Nguyen-Ha nodded.The two co-accused in relation to the shootings were sentenced earlier this year.Matthew Gempton, 36, who had pleaded guilty to manslaughter and gave evidence at Nguyen-Ha's trial, was sentenced to 12 years.Shaun Thomas Kinnane, 40, who fired at the Girrawheen and Wanneroo homes, was given seven years and six full_text: Judge jails grandfather for sexually assaulting teenage granddaughters Judge jails NSW grandfather for sexually assaulting teenage granddaughters By Zaarkacha MarlanABC Western PlainsTopic:Child Sexual AbuseFri 29 AugFriday 29 AugustFri 29 Aug 2025 at 7:32amJudge Troy Anderson sentenced the man in the District Court. (ABC News: Demi Lynch)In short: A western New South Wales man has been jailed for eight years for sexually abusing his granddaughters in 2021 and 2023.Judge Troy Anderson said the man in his 70s showed no insight into his appalling and unjustified conduct .What's next? The man was given a non-parole period of four years and six months, and will be eligible for release in 2029. abc.net.au/news/western-nsw-grandfather-jailed-sexually-abusing-grandaughters/105713086Link copiedShareShare articleTwo sisters who were sexually assaulted by their grandfather say the abuse shattered their trust, damaged their mental health and tore their family apart.WARNING: This article contains descriptions of sexual assaults some readers may find distressing.The 73-year-old western New South Wales man, who cannot be identified to protect the identity of the victims, was found guilty in March of sexually assaulting his two granddaughters in separate incidents in 2021 and 2023. Judge Troy Anderson handed down an eight-year jail sentence on Friday in the District Court and said the man showed no remorse for his appalling and unjustified conduct . The man will serve a minimum of four years and six months before being eligible for parole in 2029, and will be placed on the child protection register. Grandfather asks for 'cuddles'The court heard in 2021, the man's 14-year-old granddaughter was staying at his home when he asked her if she wanted some cuddles .The girl was on her grandfather's bed talking when he lifted her shirt and began assaulting her.Sexual assault support lines:1800 Respect National Helpline: 1800 737 732Men's Referral Service: 1300 766 491Lifeline (24-hour crisis line): 131 114Victims of Crime Helpline: 1800 819 817Full Stop Australia: 1800 385 578She told him to stop when he said: It's OK, you'll get used to it. The interaction ended when another person came into the room.However, two years later in 2023, another granddaughter, aged 13, was visiting his home when he asked her if she wanted cuddles .They were in his bedroom, where he lifted her shirt and told her she had such beautiful boobies and it was too bad he could not see them.He assaulted the girl, who tried to push him off her.He continued the assault but then stopped and said, I've made you uncomfortable, haven't I? , apologised and hugged her. Betrayed by the person they 'looked up' toOn Friday, the two girls became visibly emotional as their statements were read to the court.They expressed sadness and anger at what their pop did to them.The younger sister said what her grandfather did to her still made her sick . I remember my body going numb, and my elbows and knees going weak, she said. You were my grandfather, the man I looked up to and loved more than anything. She said when her grandfather dropped her home the next morning, she refused to say I love you , showered and scrubbed her body until it was red.She said she wrote what happened in a note on her phone. You ruined my trust, my mental health, body image and relationship with my whole family, she said. What you did is foul, disgusting and sick. You are my blood, my family and there's absolutely no excuse for what you did. The court heard that when the girl confided in her older sister, she revealed the same thing had happened to her two years earlier.She told the court her older sister produced a journal, which detailed the incident.The now 19-year-old also told the court she felt angry and overwhelmingly sad , and that her grandfather's actions tore their family apart. All this has changed me in ways I never expected. I feel betrayed by my extended family and my own pop, she said. He was my hero, my rock and supporter … why did he have to do this? I struggle to say this, but it's not my fault. He was the adult and I was the child. I wish people could understand that I'm the victim in this. I hurt and am still hurting. No explanation for 'appalling' conductJudge Anderson said the man gave bizarre and extraordinary explanations for his behaviour.In an interview with police, he did not deny what he did, but said it was all a blur, and that it was like a dream and he could suddenly smell [his granddaughters'] female scent .During the trial, the man also told the court he complimented the girls' breasts to boost their confidence. The offender considered it entirely appropriate because it boosted her confidence, and so appropriate that he repeated it years later, Judge Anderson said.Judge Anderson found the incident was not isolated and said the man still failed to grasp why he had been charged. The offender may well have believed he was giving the children some confidence through his conduct, but in my view that is just the most bizarre and extraordinary explanation for offending of this full_text: Police not ruling out potential charges against Dezi Freeman's wife and son Arrests made during search for Dezi Freeman were his wife and son, police revealTopic:CrimeFri 29 AugFriday 29 AugustFri 29 Aug 2025 at 5:36amMike Bush said more than 450 officers were part of the search, investigation, and community reassurance efforts. (ABC News)In short:Victoria Police say they arrested and later released Dezi Freeman's 42-year-old wife and 15-year-old son as part of the operation to find the alleged shooter.Chief Commissioner Mike Bush said the search area had been widened and that more than 450 officers were committed to the overall investigation.What's next?Mr Freeman remains at large, with police saying they would not leave Porepunkah until he was apprehended.abc.net.au/news/arrests-porepunkah-dezi-freeman-wife-son/105713412Link copiedShareShare articleThe two people arrested in relation to the search for alleged Porepunkah gunman Dezi Freeman were his wife and 15-year-old son, police have confirmed.Mali Freeman, 42, and the teenage boy were taken into custody during a raid at a Porepunkah home on Thursday night before being interviewed by police and released.Victoria Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush confirmed the pair were the suspected gunman's partner and son in a press conference on Friday afternoon, but did not divulge details about the basis of their arrests. People were interviewed totally and specifically in relation to the homicide investigation, he said. There may or may not be charges that follow. The search for Mr Freeman, 56, is now in its fourth day and has seen extensive police resources deployed to north-east Victoria's alpine region.Mr Freeman has been at large since allegedly fatally shooting police officers Neal Thompson and Vadim de Waart, and injuring a third, at his property on Tuesday.The shooting took place while 10 police officers were executing a search warrant for historical sex offences.The injured police officer has had surgery in hospital and remains in recovery.Over 450 officers involved in broader investigationThe town of Porepunkah is no longer under lockdown, though authorities have urged locals to remain on high alert.Until Thursday, police said they believed Mr Freeman remained in bushland surrounding the shooting site, but a dangerous person warning on the VicEmergency website was expanded up to Nagambie — 200km west of Porepunkah — on Friday.Dezi Freeman remains at large and is believed to be armed after allegedly killing two police officers in Porepunkah. (Supplied: Victoria Police)Commissioner Bush said the search area was determined on police intelligence and had been widened as we're not making any assumptions .He said more than 450 officers had been dedicated to the search operation and investigation, as well as special operators from the Australian Federal Police. Our people have every resource that they require for this horrific homicide, Commissioner Bush said. I can assure the public that there is a very professional and coordinated operation in place here to bring this to a safe conclusion … [and we want to] give the locals that assurance that we are not leaving here until this person is in custody. Commissioner Bush added that there had been alleged sightings of Mr Freeman, which police were looking into, but did not give details about where or when. We can't confirm that they are of him, but if you think you see him, let us know, we'll explore it. Police believe Mr Freeman remains armed and have urged locals to be vigilant.No terrorism links have been made to the incident so far, but Commissioner Bush said all avenues and charges would be explored once Mr Freeman was in custody.Posted Fri 29 Aug 2025 at 5:36amFriday 29 Aug 2025 at 5:36amFri 29 Aug 2025 at 5:36am, updated Fri 29 Aug 2025 at 12:07pmFriday 29 Aug 2025 at 12:07pmFri 29 Aug full_text: Suspect pours himself a beer after crashing ute into Perth shopping centre Morley Galleria damaged after car driven through shopping centre in PerthKBy Kenith PngBy Mya KordicTopic:CrimeFri 29 AugFriday 29 AugustFri 29 Aug 2025 at 4:56amLoading...In short:A ute smashed through the doors of Perth's Morley Galleria shopping centre early on Friday, causing damage inside.The driver was arrested an hour later at a nearby pub, where he allegedly broke in and poured himself a beer.What's next?The man is due to face court on several charges tomorrow, and several shops remain closed as police investigate the damage.abc.net.au/news/morley-galleria-damaged-after-car-driven-through-mall/105713252Link copiedShareShare articlePolice have charged a man in his 40s after a car was driven through the mall of one of Perth's major shopping centres, causing damage.Emergency services say they received reports of a white ute ploughing through the southern doors of the Morley Galleria shopping centre in the early hours of Friday.Police said around 4.35am the car was used to force entry into the shopping centre, after a bollard was removed.Doors at the Morley Galleria shopping centre in Perth were damaged when a car was driven through part of the shopping centre overnight. (Supplied) The vehicle has then been driven through the main doors and into the roller doors of a store, a police spokeswoman said. The driver was unable to gain entry to the store and drove back out of the shopping centre and away from the scene. Man arrested at pubAbout an hour later the man was apprehended at a nearby pub, which had yet to open.Police arrested a man inside the nearby Russell Inn. (Supplied)Police have since charged a 46-year-old Morley man with a number of offences, including criminal damage or destruction of property and aggravated burglary on a place.The pub owner told the ABC the man followed a worker who was making an early morning delivery into the venue.He said he had pretended to be a pub worker and poured himself a pint at the bar.Inside the Galleria mall on Friday morning, tyre marks were seen on the floor, while the entrance to Target had been cordoned off with white sheeting.CCTV vision shows the ute travelling through the closed mall with its headlines on.Some Morley Galleria shops remained closed on Friday after the car was driven through the centre. (Supplied)Shopping centre owners Vicinity released a statement saying several shops remain closed. Following an incident at the centre in the early hours this morning, we are currently assisting police with their investigation, the statement read. At this stage, Target has been impacted and is closed, and the entry to the Woolworths Mall will also be closed until further notice. Trading hours for some impacted stores within the Woolworths Mall may vary. All other areas of the centre remain open and trading. Workers were on the scene today, repairing the damage caused when a car drove through glass sliding doors at Morley Galleria shopping centre in Perth's east. (Supplied)Suspect 'poured himself a beer'Publican Harry Sandhu, who owns Russell Inn Bar where the suspect was arrested, said CCTV appeared to show the man driving through a wire fence near the venue and trying unsuccessfully to open the door of the pub while holding a long metal object.A fence was damaged outside the The Russell Inn Bar and Restaurant in Morley. (ABC News: Kenith Png )Another camera inside the venue appeared to show the man following a delivery worker into the venue and searching behind the bar for a glass.Upon finding one, he then pours himself a beer from the taps, before the delivery worker reappears and confronts him.The man was captured on the pub's CCTV appearing to pour himself a beer. (Supplied)The suspect then walks away from the bar and out of view, before police are seen entering the venue minutes later.When he reappears, he removes his jacket to reveal a best Dad ever apron, before putting his hands in the air, apparently at the direction of police who have tasers pointed at him.An officer is then seen handcuffing him before he is led away.Mr Sandhu said the delivery worker called police, who arrested the suspect.The Russell Inn Bar and Restaurant, where the suspect poured himself a pint after driving through Morley Galleria. (ABC News: Kenith Png )He said it was disappointing to see a family-owned business targeted. This kind of incident really makes things hard as a small business, he said.Harry Sandhu, the owner of The Russell Inn Bar and Restaurant in Morley, said it was disppaointing to see his family-run business targeted. (ABC News: Kenith Png )Mr Sandhu said his wife, who also works at the venue, was frightened after watching the CCTV footage. When she came in the morning, looking at the videos, she feels a little bit scared, he said.The Russell Inn Bar and Restaurant, where publican Harry Sandhu said the suspect poured himself a pint after driving through Morley Galleria. (ABC News: Kenith Png )The Russell Inn remained open as usual on Friday.Shopping centre woesThe incident comes as centre management continues to face sustained pressure from the community and local politicians over a long-delayed redevelopment of the shopping centre.Almost the entirety of the second floor is vacant as tenants await a $240 million renovation.A spokesperson for Vicinity said the incident was not expected to impact the centre's redevelopment plans, and it was too early to determine the cost of the damage.The accused is due to appear in Perth Magistrates Court on Saturday.He is also facing other offences on previous, unrelated matters.LoadingPosted Fri 29 Aug 2025 at 4:56amFriday 29 Aug 2025 at 4:56amFri 29 Aug 2025 at 4:56am, updated Sat 30 Aug 2025 at 12:09amSaturday 30 full_text: Witness saw missing man beaten by 'weapons and instruments', court told Bail hearing told of photos showing 'severely beaten' Brisbane man Andrew BurowBy Jessica Ross, Jake Kearnan and Owen JacquesABC Sunshine CoastTopic:Missing PersonFri 29 AugFriday 29 AugustFri 29 Aug 2025 at 4:35amPolice officers have been searching a property at Bli Bli in relation to the disappearance of Andrew Burow. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)In short: Anthony Thomas Perrett, 38, faced court today charged with torturing a Brisbane man who has been missing for more than a week.Magistrate Rod Madsen refused a bail application, saying Mr Perrett posed an unacceptable risk of offending.What's next?Mr Perrett and Billy John Howard, also charged with torturing the Brisbane man, will each face court again in October.abc.net.au/news/man-accused-of-torture-andrew-burow-denied-bail/105711436Link copiedShareShare articleA man charged with the torture of a missing Brisbane man has been denied bail after appearing in Maroochydore Magistrates Court today.Anthony Thomas Perrett, 38, has been charged with torturing Andrew Burow, 56, a cybersecurity senior manager from Kelvin Grove.The court heard police had found photos showing the severely beaten Brisbane man, who has been missing for more than a week.Brisbane man Andrew Burow, 56, has been missing from his Kelvin Grove home for more than a week (Supplied: Queensland Police)Mr Perrett's co-accused, 26-year-old North Lakes man Billy John Howard, is facing the same charge and remains behind bars.The men are accused of inflicting severe pain and suffering on the 56-year-old.Police have now established three crime scenes on the Sunshine Coast -- at Bli Bli, Pomona and Lake MacDonald.Objecting to bail, police prosecutor Jeanette Grigoris told the court there was a homicide investigation into Mr Burow's disappearance, which was ongoing and dynamic .Ms Grigoris said police had uncovered a burnt mobile phone, zip ties and alcohol wipes in a fire pit at the Bli Bli scene.An area of bushland behind a home at Bli Bli on the Sunshine Coast was taped off by police as forensic teams examined the area. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)The court heard officers also found the names of Mr Burow's parents written on a piece of paper. There is money that's been transferred to the co-accused's account, the prosecutor told the court. There is the father receiving a phone call from someone wanting money to be transferred. There is a statement from a witness who has provided evidence that she took part in a Facetime conversation where the victim was being severely beaten with weapons and instruments. The prosecutor said there was also phone data showing Mr Perrett and Mr Howard travelling with Mr Burow from August 20, when he went missing. Evidence 'extremely weak'Mr Perrett's defence lawyer Mark Williams argued the bulk of the police evidence related to the co-accused, and said the case against his client was weak . It is clear that the person at the centre of their [police] investigation is Billy Howard, he said.Defence lawyer Mark Williams says the case against his client is weak. (ABC News: Jake Kearnan) It's difficult to establish what, if any, involvement Mr Perrett has had. The strength of the evidence is extremely weak, bordering on non-existent. Police vehicles dotted a rural property outside Noosa, with police establishing a crime scene in the search for missing Brisbane man Andrew Burow. (ABC News)The court also heard Mr Perrett had been on bail for other offences including extortion, drugs and firearm charges.Mr Williams said his client had been adhering to his bail conditions.Magistrate Rod Madsen said releasing Mr Perrett on bail would be an unacceptable risk . I'm concerned if I gave you bail, there would be further offences committed, the magistrate said.Police could be seen entering and leaving a home on a rural property outside Noosa on Thursday afternoon after two new crime scenes were declared. (ABC News) Your history of offending is pretty appalling, it's pretty persistent, and involves a number of breaches of the Bail Act. Mr Perrett was remanded in custody and will return to court on October 13. full_text: 'How could you possibly do this to our family?' Impact statements read to landlord who murdered man Family of man murdered by Matthew Draganoff tells court about impact of 'violent execution'EBy Eva BlandisTopic:CourtsFri 29 AugFriday 29 AugustFri 29 Aug 2025 at 3:57amMatthew Draganoff is standing trial charged with the shooting murder of Simon Middleton at Virginia, in Adelaide's northern suburbs. Supplied. (Supplied)In short:The family of a man murdered by his landlord in 2021 has told the man responsible how the violent execution has affected them.Matthew Charles Draganoff was found guilty earlier this year of murdering Simon Middleton by shooting him three times at close range.What's next?Draganoff will be sentenced next month.abc.net.au/news/matthew-draganoff-court-family-statements/105712630Link copiedShareShare articleThe brother of a man murdered by his landlord in 2021 has told the man responsible he had taken the heart and soul of a family and could not unsee the harrowing footage of the victim's final moments.Matthew Charles Draganoff, 48, was found guilty in South Australia's Supreme Court earlier this year of murdering 49-year-old Simon Middleton by shooting him three times at close range in the early hours of March 8, 2021.The jury heard during the two-month trial that Mr Middleton was shot by Draganoff, at a property on Brady Street at Virginia, on the northern outskirts of Adelaide following growing animosity between the two.The 12-person jury handed down its verdict in June after more than 25 hours of deliberations, over five days.On Friday, the court heard 10 victim impact statements from the family and friends of Mr Middleton.His younger brother, Mark Middleton, told the court that the CCTV vision of the violent execution haunts him every day. [It] is a visual I wish I never had seen and something I cannot unsee, he said. The thought of Simon's death being a planned execution scares me. By executing Simon, you are executing the heart and soul of a family.Simon Middleton (pictured) was allegedly shot dead by Matthew Draganoff. (Supplied: SA Police) This was a cold, calculated, pre-meditated act committed by Matthew Draganoff. He chose to take a life and in doing so, he broke so many others. A victim impact statement prepared by Mr Middleton's mother Helen, and read to the court by the prosecution, outlined how the murder has affected her and her husband. You are the father of three children, how could you possibly do this to our family? she said. Because of your actions we will never have the opportunity to see or have contact with our Simon again. Lucy Boord SC, for the prosecution, outlined to the court the way Mr Middleton was murdered, and that the first shot delivered to him, with a high-powered rifle, would have been fatal — but that Mr Draganoff still delivered two more shots.The jury was told Simon Middleton was shot at a property on Brady Street, Virginia. (ABC News: Mahalia Carter) Mr Draganoff was not content with that [first shot], the second shot must have been as Simon Middleton was running for his life and Matthew Draganoff shoots him in the buttocks, and then as Simon Middleton is attempting to crawl on the ground, as is captured in that footage, Matthew Draganoff can be seen delivering the last shot to his head, she said. So, this was an execution. Ms Boord submitted to the court that Draganoff — who will ultimately receive a sentence of life imprisonment for the murder — should receive a higher non-parole period than the minimum of 20 years.Defence Barrister Michelle Barnes, for Draganoff, said her client did not accept the jury's verdict and had filed an appeal against the conviction.Draganoff will be sentenced next month.Posted
